design_detail: Systematic review with country-specific random-effects meta-analyses (Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation) of the prevalence of fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) among children and youth in the general population: 24 studies with 1416 children and youth with FASD (ages 0 to 16.4) from 8 countries, published November 1973 to June 2015, limited to active case ascertainment or clinic-based studies with a stated diagnostic guideline or case definition. The 6 countries with two or more studies were pooled; the other 181 of 187 countries, including Canada and Norway with one study each, were assigned a predicted prevalence: the drinking-during-pregnancy prevalence from Popova et al. (2017) divided by a quotient of 13 women who drank per FASD case, derived from countries with a WHO drinking-pattern score of 3 or less. Monte Carlo intervals; WHO regional and global means weighted by live births; ratios to selected special-population studies. PROSPERO CRD42016033837.
can_establish: The range of FASD prevalence found up to mid-2015 by active case ascertainment and clinic-based studies in 8 countries (below 1 to 207.5 per 1000) and pooled estimates for the 6 countries with two or more such studies, together with model-based working estimates elsewhere.
cannot_establish: Measured FASD prevalence for 181 of 187 countries, including the global and regional figures, which are predictions from self-reported and mostly modelled drinking in pregnancy; an individual's risk at any level of drinking (the 1-in-13 figure is an aggregate ratio from an unstated set of countries); effects of dose, pattern or timing; or valid comparisons between countries whose estimates differ in diagnostic system, age at assessment and ascertainment method.

sample.recruitment: MEDLINE, MEDLINE in process, EMBASE, ERIC, CINAHL, Web of Science, PsycINFO and Scopus, November 1, 1973 to June 30, 2015, without geographic or language restriction (keywords in eTable 1, not read); plus contents pages of major epidemiology journals, citation screening and contact with leading FASD experts and researchers about pending publications; non-English studies translated by fluent colleagues or with Google Translate checked by a native speaker (Methods › Comprehensive Systematic Search Strategy).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: original quantitative research in a peer-reviewed journal or scholarly report that measured FASD (or any combination of diagnoses in the spectrum), gave a CI or SE or the sample size or case count, specified the diagnostic guideline or case definition, and used active case ascertainment or clinic-based methods; no age restriction. Excluded: pooled estimates, passive surveillance, duplicate publications (Methods › Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria). No study of adults was found (Results › Comprehensive Systematic Literature Search).
sample.demographics: Table 1: study periods from 1974-1975 to 2012-2013; sample sizes 160 to 1,533,333; ages 0 to 16.4 years, with four studies of newborns or live births; percentage male 46.1 to 63.0 where reported; 18 studies used active case ascertainment, 5 were clinic-based and 1 used mixed methods; 11 of 24 (45.8%) used the clarification of the Institute of Medicine criteria. Countries: Australia 2 studies, Canada 1, Croatia 2, France 4, Italy 2, Norway 1, South Africa 6, USA 6.
sample.selection_effects: Data come from 8 countries, half the studies from South Africa and the USA; none from Asia, Latin America or the Eastern Mediterranean. The authors note that the studies were not nationally representative and that some may have been done where FASD was more prevalent; the South African studies are from selected communities in the Western and Northern Cape. Restriction to the general population removes high-prevalence groups. Two newer South African studies reporting 170 to 259 per 1000 fell outside the search window (Discussion › Strengths and Limitations, 2nd paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Maternal drinking is not extracted from the FASD studies. For prediction, each country's prevalence of any alcohol use during pregnancy is taken from Popova et al. (2017): self-reported and, for 158 of 187 countries, itself a model prediction.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not analysed: the authors state that the effect of the timing, dose and frequency of prenatal alcohol exposure on FASD risk could not be examined (Discussion › Strengths and Limitations, 1st paragraph).

comparison.controls: Not applicable (prevalence review). Special-population prevalences from select studies are expressed as multiples of the global estimate.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to prevalence. The quotient assumes the same ratio of FASD cases to women who drank in pregnancy everywhere; countries with drinking-pattern scores of 4 or 5 were left out of its derivation because they would give an unrealistically high ratio, but the resulting quotient is applied to those countries as well.

outcomes.instruments: FASD as defined in each study (Table 1): the clarification of the Institute of Medicine criteria (11 studies), Institute of Medicine criteria, the 4-digit diagnostic code, CDC diagnostic guidelines, guidelines of the Fetal Alcohol Study Group of the Research Society on Alcoholism, criteria by Sokol and Clarren, an adapted 4-digit code with American Academy of Pediatrics criteria, or a case definition stated by the authors. The breakdown into FAS, partial FAS and other diagnoses is in eTable 2 (not read).
outcomes.validity_norms: Study quality was appraised on seven criteria from a prevalence appraisal tool (representative sample, appropriate recruitment, sample of at least 300, description of participants and setting, coverage of the identified sample, objective standard criteria for FASD, appropriate statistics); results in eTable 3, not read; whether appraisal was done in duplicate is not stated. The authors state that the diagnostic systems overlap but lack diagnostic reliability and that their sensitivity and specificity are unknown (Methods › Critical Appraisal of Identified Studies; Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs).
outcomes.operationalization: FASD prevalence per 1000 children and youth in the general population, pooled by country; WHO regional and global means weighted by live births for the latest year available (2000-2014); the 630,000 annual births figure applies the global prevalence to live births.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. How studies were screened and selected, and by how many reviewers, is not reported. Extracted data were checked by one author (S.L.) against the original articles, with discrepancies reconciled by team discussion; who did the extraction is not stated (Methods › Data Extraction).

analysis.effect_sizes: Global FASD prevalence among children and youth in the general population 7.7 per 1000 (95% CI 4.9-11.7); European region 19.8 (14.1-28.0); Americas 8.8 (6.4-13.2); African region 7.8 (5.4-10.7); Western Pacific 6.7 (4.5-11.7); South-East Asia 1.4 (0.6-5.3); Eastern Mediterranean 0.1 (0.1-0.5) (Table 2). Highest countries: South Africa 111.1 (71.1-158.4; meta-analysis), Croatia 53.3 (30.9-81.2; meta-analysis), Ireland 47.5 (28.0-73.6; prediction), Italy 45.0 (35.1-56.1; meta-analysis), Belarus 36.6 (23.7-53.2; prediction); 76 of 187 countries above 1%. Quotient: one FASD case per 13 women who drank during pregnancy, about 630,000 children with FASD born each year (more than 1700 a day). Study-level prevalence (Table 1) ranges from 0.1 per 1000 (Australia, national, n = 1,533,333) and 0.4 (French newborns) to 207.5 per 1000 (South Africa, Western Cape). Special populations, as multiples of the global estimate: aboriginal 15.6 to 24.6, children in care 5.2 to 67.7, correctional 30.3, low socioeconomic status 23.7, psychiatric care 18.5 (study values 40.0 to 521.1 per 1000; Figure 2 legend). Heterogeneity and publication-bias results only in eTable 5 (not read); no prediction intervals.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42016033837 (record read): registered on 31 January 2016, after the search closed in June 2015, with a review start date of 1 May 2015; version 1.1 (11 July 2017) marks the review completed. The record planned FAS and FASD prevalence in the general population and in Aboriginal or Indigenous and other special populations, ten appraisal criteria, two-reviewer selection, and exact confidence intervals for countries with a single study. The paper appraises with seven criteria, does not report how selection was done, compares special populations through select studies rather than a systematic synthesis, predicts the two single-study countries (Canada, Norway) from drinking prevalence, and adds the quotient and the drinking-pattern exclusion, which the record does not describe. The record's synthesis text refers to alcohol consumption in pregnancy, apparently copied from the companion record.
analysis.selective_reporting: Country estimates (eTable 4), forest plots (eFigure 2), heterogeneity and publication-bias tests (eTable 5), appraisal results (eTable 3), the quotient's derivation (eMethods) and the flow diagram (eFigure 1) are only in the supplement, which was not read. Special populations were compared using select studies without stated selection criteria. Publication bias was judged unlikely in advance and would not have been adjusted for if found (Methods › Meta-analyses).
analysis.power: Country pools rest on 2 to 6 studies; which countries entered the quotient, and how many, is not stated in the main text.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 24 studies in 8 countries, FASD prevalence ranged from below 1 to 207.5 per 1000, depending on country, age, setting and method: active case ascertainment studies in the USA, Italy, Croatia and South Africa found 5.1 to 207.5 per 1000, while newborn clinic studies in France and a national Australian study found 0.1 to 5.6 per 1000. Pooled national estimates exist for 6 countries; every other figure, including the global 7.7 per 1000, is the modelled drinking prevalence divided by 13 (editors' arithmetic: 9.8% / 13 = 7.5 per 1000; European 25.2% / 13 = 19.4; Americas 11.2% / 13 = 8.6).
interpretation_gap.claimed: (1) The Key Points present "approximately 8 of 1000 in the general population had fetal alcohol spectrum disorder" and the 1-in-13 ratio as findings of a meta-analysis of 24 studies; the first is mostly a model output and the second an aggregate ratio from an unstated set of countries, not a risk for an individual pregnancy. (2) Prevalence above 1% in 76 countries is almost entirely predicted: under the quotient any country whose drinking-in-pregnancy prevalence exceeds 13% passes 1% by construction (editors' arithmetic). (3) The Discussion compares these 76 countries' FASD prevalence with US birth-defect rates (anencephaly, Down syndrome, spina bifida, trisomy 18) on the strength of those predictions. (4) The Conclusions say FASD occurs throughout society regardless of socioeconomic status, education or ethnicity; the study analysed none of these. (5) That most affected children and youth will require lifelong care, and the 630,000 births a year, are not results of this review's data. (6) Publication bias is dismissed in advance on the argument that any unexpected prevalence would be published. The limitations paragraph does state the self-report, diagnostic, representativeness and prediction problems.

timeline.event: Hoyme et al. (2005), the clarification of the 1996 Institute of Medicine criteria, used by 11 of the 24 included studies.
Popova et al. (2017), companion FAS and drinking-in-pregnancy meta-analysis by the same team from the same FAS search; its drinking estimates drive the FASD predictions here (card sc_popova_2017).
Chudley, accompanying editorial in JAMA Pediatrics (doi 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2017.2232), linked from the PMC page; not read.
May et al. (2018), Prevalence of fetal alcohol spectrum disorders in 4 US communities (JAMA 319:474; alcohol evidence map, Tier C), linked from the PMC page as related; not read in this session.

Pichini, Pacifici and Busardò, letter in JAMA Pediatrics (doi 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2018.0044) questioning that Italy was among the five countries with the highest FASD prevalence; only its opening paragraph was visible.

Lange, Rehm and Popova, reply (doi 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2018.0058): the Italian estimate (45.0 per 1000) pools two active case ascertainment studies with randomly selected schools, a diagnostic system endorsed by the Institute of Medicine and experienced dysmorphologists, 1519 children screened; the reply adds that the letter writers had raised a similar concern about the companion FAS paper.

replication.where_it_stands: The standard source for a global FASD prevalence of about 8 per 1000 children and youth and for 1 FASD case per 13 pregnancies with drinking. Only 6 national estimates are pooled from observations; all other figures, including the global and regional ones, are the companion paper's drinking-in-pregnancy prevalences divided by 13. Claims should cite study-level or country-pooled measured figures where possible (for example South Africa 111.1, Croatia 53.3 and Italy 45.0 per 1000 from active case ascertainment) and present the global figure as a model estimate. A later US four-community study (May et al., 2018) is linked from the PMC page; it was not read here. No correction is linked on the PMC or JAMA Pediatrics pages (checked 27 October 2026).

funding.funder: Not reported: neither the PMC full text nor the JAMA Pediatrics article page carries a funding statement.
funding.affiliations_note: Five of the six authors are at the Institute for Mental Health Policy Research, Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, Toronto (with University of Toronto, Technische Universität Dresden and University of New South Wales affiliations); one is at the Department of Pediatrics, University of North Dakota School of Medicine. The same team wrote Popova et al. (2017), whose estimates and methods this paper builds on. No industry funding or ties are declared.

what_would_settle_it: Active case ascertainment studies using one validated diagnostic system in randomly sampled school populations of the countries now covered only by prediction, with maternal drinking measured in the same samples, would replace modelled with measured prevalence and show how the ratio of FASD cases to exposed pregnancies varies with drinking pattern.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (children and youth in the general population), condition (FASD), outcome (prevalence) and eligible study methods are specified.

PROSPERO CRD42016033837 was registered on 31 January 2016, after the search closed (June 2015); the paper does not state that methods were set beforehand, and it departs from the record (seven instead of ten appraisal criteria, prediction instead of exact intervals for single-study countries, the quotient, special populations by select studies) without explanation.
Restriction to active case ascertainment (described as the criterion standard) and clinic-based studies, and exclusion of passive surveillance, is explained by the quality of case ascertainment.

Eight databases with keywords in a supplement, no language restriction, journal hand-searching, citation screening and contact with experts; but the search closed about 26 months before online publication (August 2017), and two newer South African studies are acknowledged as missing.
The paper does not report how screening and selection were done or by how many reviewers (the protocol planned two).
Extracted data were checked by one author against the original articles, with discrepancies reconciled by team discussion, which meets the item's consensus criterion; who extracted is not stated.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list of excluded studies with reasons appears in the article; the flow diagram (eFigure 1) is in the unread supplement.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives country and region, study period, sample size, cases, prevalence, diagnostic system, sex, age range and method; how communities or schools were chosen, participation and setting are not described.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: A prevalence-appropriate seven-criterion tool was used, but its results are only in eTable 3 (not read), duplicate appraisal is not stated, and diagnostic reliability and age at assessment are not addressed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Random-effects pooling of double-arcsine-transformed proportions is standard, but combining is not justified: newborn clinic studies are pooled with school-age active case ascertainment within countries (France: 0.4, 5.4 and 5.6 per 1000 in newborns with 66.0 on Réunion Island), studies with data from 1974 to 2013 yield estimates labelled 2012, heterogeneity is not reported in the article, there are no prediction intervals, and the observed single studies for Canada and Norway are replaced by predictions.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis of how study quality affects the pooled or predicted estimates.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The limitations discuss self-reported drinking, varying diagnostic systems, non-representative and regionally confined samples, and prediction error.
Heterogeneity tests are only in eTable 5; the article neither reports nor discusses them, although study prevalences within France range from 0.4 to 66.0 per 1000.
Tests were run (results in eTable 5), but publication bias was judged unlikely in advance and would not have been adjusted for if found; its likely impact is not discussed on the evidence.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: The authors report no conflicts of interest, which meets the item; there is, however, no funding statement at all.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are not met (2, no protocol before the review; 7, no list of excluded studies; 11, unjustified combining and unreported heterogeneity; 15, publication bias dismissed in advance) and two are only partly met (4, the search; 9, the risk-of-bias assessment); by the AMSTAR 2 rule confidence is critically low. Beyond the instrument, the global, regional and 181 of 187 national figures are not meta-analytic results but drinking prevalences divided by a single ratio. The country pools for South Africa, Croatia, Italy and the USA rest on recognized active case ascertainment studies and are the most citable numbers in the paper.

key_findings.finding: 24 unique studies were included, covering 1416 children and youth diagnosed with FASD, aged 0 to 16.4 years, from 8 countries: Australia (2 studies), Canada (1), Croatia (2), France (4), Italy (2), Norway (1), South Africa (6) and the USA (6). 18 used active case ascertainment, 5 clinic-based methods and 1 mixed methods; 45.8% used the clarification of the Institute of Medicine criteria. No study of adults was found.
key_findings.locator: Results › Comprehensive Systematic Literature Search, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Study-level FASD prevalence per 1000 (Table 1): South Africa 63.9 to 207.5 (six active case ascertainment studies, ages 4.8 to 16.4); Croatia 40.8 (urban) and 66.8 (rural); Italy 40.5 and 47.1; France 0.4, 5.4 and 5.6 in newborns (clinic-based) and 66.0 on Réunion Island (active case ascertainment); Norway 1.1; Canada 5.3; USA 5.1 to 33.5; Australia 0.1 (national, 1,533,333 children) and 1.7 (Northern Territory).
key_findings.note: The Réunion Island row prints 75 cases in 1320 children as 66.0 per 1000; 75/1320 is 56.8 per 1000 (editors' arithmetic; see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Highest country estimates per 1000: South Africa 111.1 (95% CI 71.1-158.4) and Croatia 53.3 (30.9-81.2), both by meta-analysis; Ireland 47.5 (28.0-73.6) by prediction; Italy 45.0 (35.1-56.1) by meta-analysis; Belarus 36.6 (23.7-53.2) by prediction. 76 of 187 countries had a predicted or observed prevalence above 1%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Prevalence of FASD Among Children and Youth in the General Population, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Global FASD prevalence among children and youth in the general population: 7.7 per 1000 (95% CI 4.9-11.7). By WHO region: European 19.8 (14.1-28.0), highest; Americas 8.8 (6.4-13.2); African 7.8 (5.4-10.7); Western Pacific 6.7 (4.5-11.7); South-East Asia 1.4 (0.6-5.3); Eastern Mediterranean 0.1 (0.1-0.5), lowest.

For countries with one or no study, prevalence was predicted from Popova et al.'s drinking-in-pregnancy prevalence using a quotient of women who drank per FASD case, derived only from countries with a WHO drinking-pattern score of 3 or less (countries scoring 4 or more were excluded as giving an unrealistically high ratio); the quotient is 1 FASD case per 13 women who drank, implying about 630,000 children with FASD born each year, more than 1700 a day.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Prevalence Estimation, 1st paragraph; Results › Prevalence of FASD Among Children and Youth in the General Population, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Which countries entered the quotient is given only in the eMethods (not read).

key_findings.finding: Editors' arithmetic: the regional estimates are close to the companion paper's regional drinking prevalence divided by 13 (global 9.8% / 13 = 7.5 per 1000, printed 7.7; European 25.2% / 13 = 19.4, printed 19.8; Americas 11.2% / 13 = 8.6, printed 8.8; South-East Asia 1.8% / 13 = 1.4, printed 1.4). Set against the companion FAS quotient of 1 in 67, the two papers imply about 5 FASD cases per FAS case (67 / 13 = 5.2), whereas the companion paper cites a ratio of about 9 or 10.
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic using the drinking prevalences of Popova et al. (2017), Table; the small differences come from the six meta-analysed countries.

key_findings.finding: FASD in special populations from select studies, per 1000 (Figure 2 legend): adoptees from Eastern Europe in Sweden 521.1; foster and adopted youth referred to a US children's mental health centre 285.2; a correctional population in Canada 233.5; an aboriginal population in Canada 189.7; a rural low-socioeconomic-status population in South Africa 182.4; children in a Brazilian orphanage 170.2; a US psychiatric-care population 142.4; an aboriginal population in Australia 120.4; children before adoption or in foster care in Israel 40.0. As multiples of the global estimate: 15.6 to 24.6 (aboriginal), 5.2 to 67.7 (children in care), 30.3 (correctional), 23.7 (low socioeconomic status), 18.5 (psychiatric care).
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparison of the Global Prevalence of FASD Among Children and Youth in the General Population With the Prevalence in Special Populations, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 legend

key_findings.finding: Publication bias was tested by funnel plot, rank correlation and weighted regression, but the authors judged it unlikely in advance, reasoning that any prevalence substantially different from earlier estimates would have been published, and did not adjust for it if found; test results are in eTable 5.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Meta-analyses, 1st paragraph; Results › Prevalence of FASD Among Children and Youth in the General Population, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: predictions rest on self-reported drinking in pregnancy, likely under-reported; different diagnostic guidelines and case definitions may have affected the pooled prevalence in a direction that depends on their sensitivity and specificity; not all studies were nationally representative, and some may have been done where FASD was more prevalent; predicted values carry measurement error; timing, dose and frequency of exposure could not be examined. Two newer South African studies (170 to 259 per 1000) were outside the search window.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Strengths and Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors state that current diagnostic guidelines overlap but lack diagnostic reliability owing to low convergent validity, and that their sensitivity, specificity and accuracy are unknown for lack of an external standard, which can lead to misclassification.

In a published reply to a letter questioning the Italian estimate, the authors state that Italy's 45.0 per 1000 (3.5% to 5.6%) pools two active case ascertainment studies using random selection of schools, an Institute of Medicine-endorsed diagnostic system and experienced dysmorphologists, with 1519 children screened.
key_findings.locator: JAMA Pediatrics, Global Prevalence of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder in Italy, Reply (doi 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2018.0058), 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Table 1 lists the two Italian studies with 543 and 976 children (1519 in total).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives the Réunion Island study (Serreau et al., 2002) as 75 FASD cases in 1320 children with a prevalence of 66.0 per 1000; 75/1320 is 56.8 per 1000 (editors' arithmetic). Every other row of Table 1 reproduces from its cases and sample size.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the sample size or the prevalence is misprinted (66.0 per 1000 would need about 1136 children); the French pooled estimate may carry the error. The same values appear on the JAMA Pediatrics page.

reporting_issues.issue: Passive surveillance was an exclusion criterion, yet Harris and Bucens (2003, Australia, Northern Territory) is included with a method described as mixed methods (passive surveillance and clinic based).
reporting_issues.consequence: The inclusion criteria were not applied strictly; Australia's pooled estimate partly rests on surveillance data.

reporting_issues.issue: Elliott et al. (2008), a national Australian study of 1,533,333 children with 92 cases (0.06 per 1000, editors' arithmetic), is classed as active case ascertainment, which the paper defines as researchers actively seeking, assessing and identifying cases; its prevalence is 18 to more than 3000 times lower than in the other active case ascertainment studies (1.1 to 207.5 per 1000; editors' arithmetic), and how cases were found is not described.
reporting_issues.consequence: The method label may group very different ascertainment designs; Australia's pooled estimate depends on it.

reporting_issues.issue: The two countries with a single study, Canada (5.3 per 1000) and Norway (1.1 per 1000), are assigned predicted values, which are given only in eTable 4; the main text does not show how far the predictions depart from the observed values.
reporting_issues.consequence: Observed data are set aside in favour of a model for these two countries, contrary to the registered plan of reporting single studies with exact intervals.

reporting_issues.issue: The Figure 2 legend gives FASD in a Brazilian orphanage (Strömland et al.) as 170.2 per 1000, while the companion paper by the same team (Popova et al., 2017, Discussion, 3rd paragraph) gives FAS in the same orphanage as 3191 per 10,000 (319.1 per 1000), although FAS is a subset of FASD.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one of the two figures is wrong; neither should be cited without checking the primary study.

reporting_issues.issue: No funding statement appears in the PMC full text or on the JAMA Pediatrics article page.
reporting_issues.consequence: Funding cannot be recorded; the companion paper reports institutional funding by the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health only.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC5710622 (publisher's version; all sections, Tables 1 and 2 rendered as text, figure legends, article notes, author contributions and disclosures read; Figure 1 (map) and Figure 2 (special-population comparison) are images, and values were taken only from the text and the Figure 2 legend; the supplement (eTables 1 to 6, eMethods, eFigures 1 and 2; PDF) was not read). PROSPERO record CRD42016033837 read. The JAMA Pediatrics page (doi 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2017.1919) was checked: no correction is linked; the linked letter (Pichini et al., doi 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2018.0044) showed only its opening paragraph, and the opening paragraph of the authors' reply (doi 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2018.0058) was read.
